caption:
OpenAI says it found a hidden recording device in an executive conference room in San Francisco.
The company says its own AI models helped trace the device to an employee, who was fired and arrested by the FBI.
OpenAI says it sees no sign that model weights, source code or customer data were taken.

Should AI labs use their own AI to investigate their staff?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: TechCrunch · Photo: U.S. Department of Justice

slides.headline: OpenAI found a *hidden bug* in its executive room. Its own AI traced it to an employee

slides.heading: Hidden in *toilet paper*
paras: OpenAI staff found a recording device on September 30, plugged into a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room in San Francisco.
It was wrapped in toilet paper. The device was installed around September 28, and its contents were encrypted, according to the Justice Department.

slides.heading: The AI *detective*
paras: OpenAI says it used its own models to understand the device and where it came from, identifying a specific employee who had planted it a few days earlier.
The company has not explained what exactly its models analyzed. It referred the case to the FBI.

slides.heading: Fired and *arrested*
paras: The Justice Department named the engineer as Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national who joined OpenAI in July 2025. He was arrested on October 9.
He is charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. These are allegations, and he has not been convicted.

slides.heading: No sign of *stolen secrets*
paras: OpenAI says it has no indications that he accessed or took model weights, source code or customer data.

paras.t: Prosecutors say security found a second recording device in a bag he left behind on October 5.

slides.hook: AI labs now guard their meeting rooms like spy agencies. Follow for what the FBI finds next.
